Article | Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-77118-7 Mesoscale proximity labeling at chromatin leads to identiﬁcation of small molecule mechanism of action

Cameron J. Douglas 1,2,5, Preston Samowitz 1,2,5, Feifei Tong1, Alice Long3, Caitlin M. Bradley1, Laszlo Radnai 1, David W. C. MacMillan 3, Courtney A. Miller1,2, Gavin Rumbaugh 1,2 & Ciaran P. Seath 1,2,4

Proximity labeling typically identiﬁes interactomes of single protein or RNA baits, limiting its use for mechanisms distributed across molecular systems. Here, we establish MesoMap, a chromatin-focused mesoscale proximitylabeling strategy that installs nanoscale photocatalysts on multiple histone baits to monitor drug-induced redistribution of proteins near chromatin. MesoMap captured HDAC inhibitor-induced remodeling of chromatinassociated proteins and, in a proof-of-concept de-orphaning application, prioritized a chromatin-proximal CLK/splicing axis for SR-1815, a phenotypically discovered SynGAP-restoring small molecule. Integration with kinase assays, splicing analysis, inhibitor comparisons, and published neuronal validation supports a model in which SR-1815 regulates SynGAP abundance through polypharmacological kinase modulation, including CLK-dependent effects on splicing. Together, these studies establish MesoMap as a complementary approach for resolving drug-induced protein redistribution near chromatin and accelerating mechanism-of-action studies for phenotypic chemical probes.

Changes in chromatin architecture are a critical part of cellular regulation and control adaptive responses to external stimuli. Sequencing-based methods that interrogate changes in chromatin structure such as ATAC-seq and Hi–C have become mainstay techniques in molecular and cellular biology for interrogating genomic accessibility (ATAC-seq), and genome-wide looping interactions (Hi- C), but because they rely on nucleic acid readouts they can only infer protein localization1,2. Chromatin immunoprecipitation enables direct visualization of genomic localization for a single target protein, but it is limited by antibody availability and is cost-prohibitive at scale. Mass-spectrometry-based chromatin proteomics has emerged in parallel to address a complementary question: which proteins occupy chromatin in a given cellular state3. Subcellular fractionation strategies (crude fractionation, ChEP, DEMAC) and differential extraction

approaches (differential MNase, salt fractionation, gradient-seq) recover the bulk chromatin-bound proteome and can resolve euchromatic from heterochromatic compartments, but they require biochemical disruption of the nucleus and report a static, ensembleaveraged snapshot rather than native interactions captured in living cells3. Antibody-dependent strategies including ChIP-MS, RIME and qPLEX-RIME, and ChIP-SICAP enrich the local proteome around a single bait protein or modiﬁcation, but they are constrained by 1) antibody availability and quality, 2) by epitope masking that can occlude the very interactions of interest, and 3) by the need to predeﬁne the target4–9. When applied to chromatin, the dominant biotinylation-based PL approaches (BioID, TurboID, APEX2 fused to histones or chromatin associated proteinsfactors) capture weak and transient interactions in their native context without depending on antibody pulldown, but they either operate on hour-long timescales that limit temporal resolution or label across radii that do not cleanly distinguish chromatinbound from nucleoplasmic proteins12. Reader-domain–based afﬁnity probes such as ChromID extend PL to PTM-deﬁned chromatin regions, but the engineered binders can compete with endogenous readers for the same modiﬁcation and sample only the sub-population they recognize13. Across these approaches, the single-bait design limits their utility for assessing a stimulus with an unknown mechanism, such as a bioactive ligand from a phenotypic screen. A method that captures protein occupancy dynamics across the entire face of chromatin would provide mechanistic insights into how bioactive ligands alter transcriptional states. To realize such a goal, two challenges must be addressed. First, the labeling radius must be short enough to distinguish chromatin-bound proteins from the bulk nuclear proteome. This is a constraint that long-radius PL methods

such as APEX2 and BioID cannot meet, although they are useful for studying translocation of proteins and RNA between organelles14,15. We previously showed that the shorter effective labeling radius of the carbene-based μMap chemistry resolves chromatin interactions that APEX-based histone PL cannot16. Second, no single-bait PL experiment can simultaneously sample chromatin’s structurally and functionally heterogeneous compartments with the temporal resolution needed to follow ligand-induced redistribution. Based on the efﬁcacy of our previous work studying the histone microenvironments with a µMap photo-proximity labeling platform, we questioned whether µMap could be adapted to study protein occupancy across the entirety of chromatin, an approach we term mesoscale proximity labeling, or MesoMap. In principle, this could be accomplished by incorporating µMap photo-proximity labeling catalysts throughout chromatin using multiple baits, which would enable measurements of changes across all of chromatin, rather than at a speciﬁc nuclear protein; similar to prior studies where multiple baits were used to study cell synapses, organelles, or membrane (Fig. 1A)17–19. If successful, this strategy would provide a broad chromatin-proximal readout of how cellular stimuli change molecular interactions that lead to transcriptional phenotypes.

Phenotypic screening can identify bioactive small molecules that regulate disease-relevant cellular states, but such probes often remain mechanistically orphaned because their effects arise from coordinated changes across multiple targets and pathways rather than a single predeﬁned target. Standard abundance-based proteomics and literature curation can identify candidate pathways, but they may not reveal whether candidate proteins are redistributed to or from functional chromatin-proximal environments. We reasoned that strategy for MesoMap of chromatin could complement conventional de-orphaning methods by identifying proteins whose occupancy near chromatin changes in response to a bioactive compound, thereby prioritizing mechanistic axes for biochemical and transcript-level follow-up.

Results Development of pc293T cell line We generated a HEK293T cell line stably expressing four histones bearing CfaN fusions in addition to free GFP for selection: H2A, H3.1, H3.3, and H4. Histones H2A and H4 provide spatial differences within a single nucleosome, while H3.1 and H3.3 are incorporated into different regions of chromatin. This strategy should provide a reasonable distribution of photocatalysts throughout the entirety of chromatin and they would be positioned to label only chromatin bound proteins through nanoscale photo-proximity labeling (Fig. 1B). To incorporate the histones uniformly, we utilized the MultiMam expression cassette bearing all of the CfaN tagged histones and propagated single cell clones20. After expansion, colonies underwent ﬂow cytometry to select a cell line with uniform, high expression of GFP (Supplementary Fig. 1A), referred to as pc293T herein. Isolation of biochemically intact nuclei from pc293T cells enabled rapid intein splicing using CfaCbiotin (Fig. 2A, B), in addition to the iridium photocatalyst conjugated CfaC after 30 mins (Supplementary Fig. 1B). Catalyst conjugated chromatin was shown to undergo photocatalytic proximity labeling in a light and probe dependent manner (Fig. 2C). Confocal microscopy of pc293T cells showed exclusive nuclear localization of the ﬂuorescently labeled histone constructs (Fig. 2D). Distribution of the histone constructs throughout chromatin was validated by CUT&TAG sequencing using anti-FLAG and anti-H3.3 antibodies as well as MNase-seq of the pc293T cells. Comparing FLAG and mononucleosome peaks, our construct is shown to overlap with less than 0.2% of nucleosomes (Fig. 2E, F). Global proteomics of pc293T cells shows the abundance of CfaN tagged histones to be 0.37% of all nucleosomes (Supplementary Fig. 1C and Supplementary Data 1). Additionally, 25.7% of the FLAG peaks overlap with H3.3 and share similar distribution throughout gene bodies (Fig. 2G, H and Supplementary Fig. 1D and F). Further, CUT&TAG of the chromatin markers H3K27me3 and H3K27ac reveal a closer alignment of FLAG to the euchromatin marker H3K27ac (Supplementary Fig. 1E), indicating that CfaN-tagged histone incorporation is biased toward more accessible euchromatic regions, while still showing partial overlap with H3K27me3-marked heterochromatin. Together these data validate the incorporation of our histone constructs into nucleosomes with a distribution that samples both compartments, albeit with a quantitative bias toward euchromatin. Proximity proteomics was conducted to validate that our method provides a distinctive chromatin interactome rather than capturing the bulk nuclear proteome. First, we compared the streptavidin enriched MesoMap labeled proteins to background streptavidin enriched proteins. We irradiated biochemically intact nuclei, either containing CfaC-Ir conjugated chromatin or no CfaC-Ir incorporation, in the presence of 200 µM diazirine-biotin for 60 seconds. Excess diazirinebiotin was washed out prior to lysis and streptavidin enrichment. We compared the two enriched proteomes to identify MesoMap streptavidin enriched proteins using TMT-multiplexed proteomics. This revealed an enrichment of histones, chromatin associated proteins, and histone binding proteins along with broad coverage of known chromatin associated complexes (Fig. 2I, J and Supplementary

Data 2–3). Gene ontology further reveals some of the top terms associated with the streptavidin enriched proteins include chromosome organization, DNA metabolic process, and ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling (Fig. 2J). Of the 1422 proteins signiﬁcantly enriched, 1124 are annotated as nuclear; those not annotated nuclear are predominately associated with the mitochondria, ER, or unannotated proteins (Supplementary Fig. 2A–C). These contaminants are frequently seen in our datasets and are a product of the cationic properties of the iridium photocatalyst paired with imperfect nuclear isolation21,22. If desired, these mitochondrial and ER proteins can be ﬁltered out of the dataset post-hoc, but, when conducting comparative analysis of drug vs vehicle, these background labeled proteins are innately ﬁltered out as they are labeled at the same rate in both treatment groups. Further, this experiment shows good coverage of the annotated genes for the nuclear proteome, chromatin associated proteome, histone binding proteins, and a variety of chromatin remodeling complexes (Supplementary Fig. 2D–E). Next, we compared the nuclear proteome with labeled proteins from our mesoscale protocol (Supplementary Fig. 3A). Here, the MesoMap protocol provides a distinct interactome from the nuclear proteome (Supplementary Fig. 3A and Supplementary Data 4–5). We identiﬁed several epigenetic and chromatin remodeling complexes, and although the distribution of CfaN-histones is biased toward euchromatin, the MesoMap proteome included proteins associated with both heterochromatin and euchromatin compartments (Supplementary Fig. 2E and 3B), indicating that heterochromatin-resident factors are sampled, albeit at reduced relative depth. GO analysis of the proteins enriched in our PL samples also showed enrichment of chromatin related terms such as chromatin remodeling and mitotic cell cycle (Supplementary Fig. 3C). Conversely, GO terms associated with RNA metabolism were enriched in the bulk nuclear samples, supporting our hypothesis that our carbene based proximity labeling protocol cannot diffuse through the bulk nuclear milieu (Supplementary Fig. 3C). Incorporation of histone constructs had a moderate impact on cell morphology, global protein expression, proliferation, and nucleosome occupancy in pc293T relative to WT HEK293T cells, although no change in drug sensitivity was observed (Supplementary Fig. 4A–F). We hypothesize that these changes could be attributed to either the incorporation of our constructs or through the single cell selection process which would naturally lead to bias towards proliferative phenotypes. However, we believe these minor observed differences in pc293T and HEK293T cells are inconsequential as this platform is applied to comparative proteomics within the same cell line and observing the impact of external stimuli on chromatin.

The impact of HDAC inhibitors on chromatin occupancy of epigenetic complexes We next sought to test our method by measuring chromatin state changes induced by treatment with the histone deacetylase inhibitor, romidepsin (Fig. 3A, B). Romidepsin promotes histone acetylation by inhibiting multiple deacetylase enzymes, leading to a more open chromatin state and altered transcriptional signatures23. This mechanistic paradigm has been proposed as a treatment for many indications, including neurological diseases, several cancers, and HIV23–25. First, we ensured romidepsin treatment maintains a phenotypic effect on pc293T cells. Agreeing with prior reports, we saw signiﬁcant changes in histone acetylation when treating at 10 nM as measured by changes in acetylation at H3K9/14 (Supplementary Fig. 5A)26. Further, pc293T cells were sensitive to romidepsin, leading to a signiﬁcant decrease in proliferation after a 72 h treatment (Supplementary Fig. 5B). Global changes in nuclear protein abundance were quantiﬁed in parallel (Supplementary Fig. 5C–D and Supplementary Data 6–12). A central feature of MesoMap is its ability to detect altered chromatin interactions arising from protein redistribution that is independent of expression, while concurrently capturing occupancy changes that track with altered protein abundance within the same dataset. This is most apparent at 6 h, where extensive remodeling of chromatin occupancy occurred with minimal changes in nuclear protein levels (Supplementary Fig. 5C). By 24 h, the two measurements showed stronger correlation (Supplementary Fig. 5D), reﬂecting accumulating expression changes that are themselves captured by MesoMap. Analysis of enriched proteins at 6 h revealed proteins recruited and displaced from chromatin were consistent with changes in histone acetylation (Fig. 3C). Speciﬁcally, we note the recruitment of bromodomain containing epigenetic readers BRD2, BRD4, and TRIM33 after 6 hours. Bromodomain readers bind acetylated H4 and H3 broadly, and their recruitment is consistent with the changes in histone acetylation induced by romidepsin treatment. We also observed enrichment of components of the NuRD (MTA, MBD3, GATAD2) and MiDAC (DNTTIP1, MIDEAS) histone deacetylase complexes, although no differential enrichment of the HDAC proteins were observed. These complexes are recruited to open regions of chromatin through a variety of histone and DNA binding domains (e.g., WD40, BAH) present in their non-HDAC components. Their inclusion in our data suggests that recruitment of these complexes to chromatin is independent of HDAC function and is primarily regulated by chromatin state. Furthermore, we observe the displacement of histone methyl transferases DOT1L, and KMT5C in response to romidepsin treatment. Crosstalk between DOT1L and HDAC1 has been reported in both yeast and mammalian cell lines with context dependent effects on transcription and histone post-translational state, although the precise nature of their interplay remains unknown27–29. KMT5C (SUV420H2) stably associates with repressed heterochromatin via H3K9me3 and promotes a compacted chromatin state30. As romidepsin treatment and the development of hyperacetylation leads to less compact chromatin and a substantial increase in H3K9ac, this may account for the loss of KMT5C binding. These interactions were validated through proximity ligation assays (PLA), which required antibodies for the proteins of interest and FLAG for the inserted histone constructs, which together showed robust interaction changes that matched our PL (Fig. 3D, E and Supplementary Fig. 5E–F). Comparing chromatin occupancy with nuclear protein abundance for the top hits, MIDEAS, KMT5C, and DOT1L showed minimal change in nuclear protein levels, indicating that their altered chromatin engagement reﬂects redistribution rather than changes in expression or stability (Fig. 3F). TRIM33 showed an increase in both chromatin occupancy and nuclear protein abundance, consistent with coordinated regulation of expression and recruitment, and we interpret the chromatin-occupancy signal in this case as a combined readout of both processes rather than purely physical recruitment or change in expression. To correlate changes in chromatin occupancy with function, we next assessed changes in post-translational states associated with proteins where romidepsin treatment is known to regulate chromatin binding. We ﬁrst blotted for various acetylation sites on histone H3, which would correlate HDAC inhibition with recruitment of bromodomain containing proteins, leading to a subsequent loss of methylated lysine readers. In line with literature reports, increased acetylation at histones H3K9/14, H3K23, H3K27, and H4K20 was observed (Fig. 3G and Supplementary Fig. 6A–D)26,31. A robust decrease in H3K79 methylation (via H3K79me3) was observed over time, consistent with a loss of DOT1L-histone interactions (Fig. 3H and Supplementary Fig. 6E–G)32. Analysis of the data for enriched sets of genes

that constitute epigenetic complexes showed displacement of PRC1.1, a non-canonical polycomb complex that mediates ubiquitylation of H2A via RING1, independent of PRC2 and H3K27me3 (Supplementary Fig. 5G)33,34. Immunoblotting for H2AK119Ub following romidepsin treatment showed a gradual decrease in this mark over 24 h treatment, and no change to H3K27me3 over same time course, signifying a mechanism where PRC1.1 is directed to chromatin through KDM2 (Fig. 3I and Supplementary Fig. 6H–I)33,35. Thus, MesoMap broadly captures distinct protein complexes, while still retaining sufﬁcient resolution to distinguish an individual protein’s engagement with chromatin, highlighting the utility of our approach. Comparing chromatin occupancy of epigenetic remodeling complexes over time showed dynamic changes in chromatin interactions. Recruitment of NuRD, SWI/SNF, and ATAC complex members is observed at 6 h, though the majority of the members of these complexes were displaced from chromatin by 24 h (Supplementary Fig. 5H). NuA4, Swr1, B-WICH, and Ino80 were progressively displaced from chromatin over time, with small changes observed at 6 h that grew in magnitude over the next 18 h. These data illustrate the platform’s ability to track changes in chromatin occupancy over time in response to extracellular stimulus. Critically, µMap applied to any single histone, or by combinations of fewer than four histones, captured only a partial chromatin interactome with many interactions restricted to a single histone variant, illustrating the necessity of distributing photocatalysts across all four histones; chromatin fractionation protocols similarly failed to recover these altered interactions, consistent with known limitations of biochemical fractionation including loss of weakly chromatin-associated proteins during extraction, cross-contamination between nucleoplasmic and chromatin fractions, and the inability to capture short-lived occupancy events (Supplementary Fig. 7, Supplementary Fig. 8 and Supplementary Data 13–20)3.

Transcriptional changes in response to HDACi After 24 h treatment of romidepsin, we observed changes in the chromatin occupancy of several classes of transcription factors, including AP-1, GATA, and the Yamanaka factors SOX2 and KLF3 (Fig. 3J). In contrast to chromatin-modifying enzymes and reader proteins, whose recruitment to chromatin is driven by changes in histone PTMs, transcription factors would presumably be recruited via either opening of speciﬁc regions of chromatin, or by molecular changes to their own structure, e.g., post-translational modiﬁcation or scaffolding interactions. Recruitment of AP-1 members ATF3 and JUN supports observations previously made via ATAC-seq in HDACi treated patient samples36. Based on these correlations, we validated the recruitment and displacement of a subset of enriched proteins associated with histone acetylation (displaced: P300, HDAC1) and AP-1 transcription (Recruited: ATF3) using PLA (Fig. 3K and Supplementary Fig. 9). Subsequently, we performed secondary validation with a DNA binding activity ELISA assay for ATF3 and other AP-1 proteins (Fig. 3L and Supplementary Fig. 10A). As many transcription factors are regulated via phosphorylation, we questioned whether transcription factor phosphorylation was promoted by romidepsin treatment leading to recruitment to chromatin37,38. Western blotting of treated samples showed an increase in both tyrosine and serine/threonine phosphorylation following 24 h treatment (Supplementary Fig. 10B). Phosphoproteomics analysis provided a total of 2984 nuclear phosphosites with 1954 of these being signiﬁcantly regulated in response to 24 h romidepsin treatment (Supplementary Fig. 10C and Supplementary Data 21–24). Several members of the AP-1 transcription factor family were phosphorylated in response to romidepsin treatment, including c-JUN (S243, S73), JUND (S90, S100) and ATF3 (T162) (Supplementary Fig. 10C–D), suggesting romidepsin-induced phosphorylation is responsible for transcriptional regulation of AP-1 genes through recruitment to chromatin

Deconvolution of the orphaned drug candidate SR-1815 The small molecule SR-1815 was recently discovered using a phenotypic screening platform that identiﬁes agents that regulate the abundance of endogenous proteins44. SR-1815 was subsequently validated through the Endo-GeneScreen platform as a drug-like small molecule that restores SynGAP abundance in Syngap1 haploinsufﬁ- cient neurons and mitigates disease-relevant synaptic and neuronal phenotypes. In thatstudy, SR-1815 restored SynGAP abundance toward wildtype levels, produced a pronounced increase in synaptic SynGAP, and showed genotype-dependent effects on neuronal function. Because SYNGAP1 Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy (SYNGAP1-DEE) is caused by reduced SynGAP protein expression in brain cells45,46, the SR-1815 scaffold is positioned as a potential candidate for treating this genetic neurodevelopmental disorder. However, because SR-1815 is a previously uncharacterized small molecule discovered through phenotypic screening, the molecular mechanisms underlying its effects remain unknown, limiting its potential as a preclinical drug candidate. Here, we used MesoMap to address a complementary question: how an orphaned phenotypic hit with established neuronal activity and therapeutic potential could be mechanistically deconvoluted through chromatin-proximal proteomics. To evaluate the suitability of SR-1815 for the MesoMap platform, we ﬁrst determined how and to what extent this probe regulates transcription. Indeed, we found that SR-1815 dramatically regulates gene expression in cells. For example, treating cortical neurons for 4 h led to hundreds of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), while thousands of DEGs were detected after a two-week treatment (Supplementary Data 25–28). A workﬂow that combined RNA-seq with standard proteomics revealed that differentially expressed transcripts were highly correlated with accompanying changes in protein abundance (Fig. 4A, B, Supplementary Fig. 12A, and Supplementary Data 25, 26, 29, 30). Thus, SR-1815 reorganizes the neuronal proteome by altering transcriptional dynamics. An analysis of biological pathways suggested that both acute and longer-term SR-1815 treatments regulate neuronal development, cytoskeletal dynamics, synapse biology, and mRNA processing, as well as signaling pathways traditionally linked to these cellular processes (Fig. 4C–E and Supplementary Fig. 12B–C). We conﬁrmed that SR-1815 regulated these cellular processes and neuronal structures. For example, a SynGO analysis indicated that postsynaptic biology was disproportionately impacted by both the short and longer-term SR-1815 treatment (Fig. 4C–E and Supplementary Fig. 12B). Indeed, expression of some postsynaptic proteins, including SynGAP, PSD95, and GluN1 were elevated, while others were not, including several presynaptic proteins (Fig. 4F, G). Consistent with an increase in postsynaptic protein abundance, dendritic spine size was also increased (Fig. 4H). Furthermore, SR-1815 regulated cytoskeletal dynamics linked to neuronal differentiation, as evidenced by more elaborated dendrites with increased total

MAP2 signal, a protein expressed within dendritic microtubules (Fig. 4I, J). To determine the molecular mechanism of SR-1815, we ﬁrst embarked on a classical target identiﬁcation campaign, beginning with photoafﬁnity labeling. Although the structure activity relationship around SR-1815 was shown to be relatively narrow, synthetic modiﬁcations around the SR-1815 scaffold suggested that the cyclopentyl group appended to the pyrazole unit may be able to be replaced to accommodate a linear diazirine containing alkyl chain. We synthesized the diazirine containing scaffold, SR-1815-diazirine, and assessed its ability to upregulate SynGAP in our neuronal assay to ensure the modiﬁcation retained on target activity. We observed no upregulation after 14 days, suggesting that modiﬁcation for PAL or enrichment type target ID may not be a viable option (Fig. 5A). We next attempted thermal proteome proﬁling (TPP), a method our group has had success with in the past, in both neurons and HEK293T cells to identify common binding partners (Supplementary Fig. 13 and Supplementary Data 31–33)47. These approaches led to a small number of hits in both neurons and HEK293T cells but with no overlapping IDs between cell lines (Fig. 5B). Furthermore, the proteins identiﬁed had no clear relationship to the observed phenotype. Although photoafﬁnity labeling and thermal proteome proﬁling were not exhaustively optimized, neither approach provided a coherent target hypothesis for SR-1815. Because SR-1815 induced transcriptional and proteomic changes enriched for neuronal development, synapse biology, cytoskeletal regulation, and mRNA processing, we hypothesized that its activity might involve molecular processes occurring at or near chromatin. We therefore reasoned that MesoMap could provide mechanistic information not readily obtained from ligand-enrichment strategies or abundance-based proteomics alone. To test this, we performed MesoMap on pc293T cells treated with SR-1815. In contrast, matched whole-proteome analysis under the same treatment conditions identiﬁed only 19 proteins with signiﬁcant abundance changes (Fig. 5D and SupplementaryData 34–37). Thus, SR- 1815 produced a substantially broader remodeling of chromatinassociated protein occupancy than was apparent from bulk protein abundance alone. To deﬁne the added value of MesoMap for SR-1815 de-orphaning, we compared the MesoMap proﬁle with the matched whole-proteome dataset and asked which candidate mechanisms would be prioritized by abundance-level changes alone. Whole-proteome analysis identi- ﬁed a limited set of protein abundance changes but did not, by itself, resolve the chromatin-proximal redistribution of CLK-family kinases and RNA-processing factors. By contrast, MesoMap showed altered chromatin association of CLK1/2/3/4 together with RNA-splicing machinery, thereby prioritizing a kinase–splicing axis for biochemical and transcript-level follow-up and reducing ambiguity relative to abundance-based proﬁling alone. Speciﬁcally, MesoMap detected recruitment of CLK1/3/4 to chromatin together with RNA-splicing machinery, while CLK2 was displaced from chromatin (Fig. 5C, D). We also observed recruitment of c-JUN and the Rho GTPase CDC42, along with displacement of the calcium/calmodulin-regulated kinase CaMKII. These proteins are major regulators of neuronal development and synapse biology and are therefore consistent with the observed effects of SR-1815 on dendritic morphogenesis, dendritic spine structure, and expression of synapse-targeted proteins48–51. SR-1815 is a multi-kinase inhibitor The ﬁndings above support a model in which SR-1815 inhibits CLK1/2, reduces SR-protein phosphorylation, and alters splicing in a manner that contributes to increased Syngap1/SynGAP abundance. However, the temporal separation between acute splicing changes and the longer-term Syngap1 poison-exon response, together with the broader neuronal response to SR-1815, suggested that CLK inhibition may contribute to, but not fully explain, the compound’s activity. Consistent with CLK inhibition contributing to SynGAP regulation, TG003, a chemically distinct CLK-family inhibitor, enhanced SynGAP expression, but was less efﬁcacious than SR-1815 (Fig. 6D)58. This partial phenocopy supports CLK involvement while indicating that SR-1815 efﬁcacy is unlikely to be explained by CLK inhibition alone. Because small-molecule kinase inhibitors frequently engage more than one target, we next asked whether SR-1815 acts through a broader kinase target matrix. We screened SR-1815 across a kinome-wide binding panel to deﬁne its kinase engagement proﬁle59. A measure of kinase inhibitor selectivity showed that SR-1815 engaged <8% of the kinome (Fig. 6E and Supplementary Fig. 14A, and Supplementary Data 40), positioning it as a relatively selective multi-kinase inhibitor with similarities to several

FDA-approved cancer therapeutics (Supplementary Fig. 14B). As expected, SR-1815 strongly engaged CLK1/2 in this assay (Fig. 6E and Supplementary Fig. 14A). Additional activity was observed across six kinase families (Supplementary Fig. 14B), with high-afﬁnity targets in the receptor tyrosine kinase family, including KIT, FLT1, FLT3, TrkA/ TrkB, PDGFRβ, and CSF1R. In-cell kinase occupancy proﬁling further conﬁrmed SR-1815 binding to kinases in cells (Supplementary Fig. 14C–F and Supplementary Data 41–44). To determine whether kinase targets beyond CLK1/2 could contribute to SynGAP regulation, we mined several databases to identify small molecules known to inhibit one or more SR-1815 targets and tested their ability to upregulate SynGAP (Fig. 6F, G). Sunitinib exhibited strong activity in the SynGAP expression assay, whereas the other tested inhibitors either had no effect or reduced assay activity (Fig. 6G)60. Whereas these other inhibitors shared at least one highafﬁnity target with SR-1815, only sunitinib shared high-afﬁnity targets across multiple kinase families, including receptor tyrosine kinases, STE-family kinases, and CDK/MAPK/GSK/CLK-family kinases within the CMGC group (Fig. 6F and Supplementary Fig. 14B)61. This pattern suggests that SynGAP upregulation is not explained by inhibition of a single shared target, but instead may require coordinated engagement of multiple kinase pathways. SR-1815 was more efﬁcacious than sunitinib in the SynGAP expression assay (Fig. 6G). This difference is not simply explained by broader kinase engagement, because SR-1815 is more selective than sunitinib (Supplementary Fig. 14B). Instead, the enhanced activity of SR-1815 may reﬂect its distinct target matrix. Among targets that distinguish SR-1815 from sunitinib, TrkA/TrkB were notable. TrkB-Fc, which attenuates TrkB signaling, increased the SynGAP assay signal by ~20% (Fig. 6G). This partial effect suggests that TrkB-related signaling may contribute to SR-1815 efﬁcacy, but, like TG003, does not fully phenocopy SR-1815. Discussion Proximity labeling has become a mainstay method in molecular biology for understanding the interactomes of speciﬁc proteins in a native environment. Our approach provides evidence that PL can be used for unbiased discovery of ligand-induced changes to chromatin occupancy. This application of PL assigns a molecular ﬁngerprint to a speciﬁc cellular stimulus that, in many cases, is more data rich than global analysis of expressed genes. Existing chromatin proteomic and genomic approaches, including chromatin fractionation, ChIP-based methods, ChIP-MS/RIME-style workﬂows, and proximity-labeling strategies, provide powerful but distinct views of chromatin biology. These methods differ in antibody dependence, locus speciﬁcity, labeling radius, temporal resolution, and ability to distinguish

chromatin-proximal redistribution from bulk abundance changes. MesoMap is intended to complement these approaches by providing a rapid, proximity-based readout of stimulus-induced changes in proteins associated with chromatin. Beyond proving the approach is possible, MesoMap provided molecular insights into how chromatin is regulated in response to HDAC inhibition. These mesoscale changes to protein localization can also be combined with other ‘omics techniques to generate mechanistic hypotheses. For example, comparison of phosphopeptides with proteins enriched by MesoMap revealed correlations between localization and phosphorylation of the AP-1 and B-WICH complexes (Supplementary Fig. 10C–G)64,65.

MesoMap also provided a mechanism-prioritization strategy for de-orphaning SR-1815, a phenotypically discovered SynGAP-restoring probe44. In this application, MesoMap detected altered chromatin association of CLK-family kinases and RNA-splicing machinery, prioritizing a kinase/splicing axis that was subsequently supported by ADP- Glo kinase assays, SR-protein phosphorylation changes, neuronal splicing analysis, and inhibitor-comparison experiments. Rather, it provided chromatin-proximal information that helped prioritize candidate mechanisms not apparent from abundance-based proteomics alone. The SR-1815 application also illustrates an important feature of phenotypic probe de-orphaning, where biologically active compounds may produce both proximal target-dependent effects and longer-term adaptive cell-state remodeling. For 4 h treatments, 50% of media was replaced with fresh feeding media on DIV 3, 7, and 10. On DIV 14 cultures were supplied vehicle or SR-1815 at 4.4 µM for 4 h through 50% media exchange. On DIV 14 media was removed and 20 µL of DNA/RNA Shield (Zymo: R1100-50) was added to each well. Total RNA was submitted to The Herbert Wertheim UF Scripps Institute for Biomedical Innovation & Technology - Genomics Core (RRID:SCR_017827), where it was quantiﬁed using a Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA) and evaluated on an Agilent 4200 TapeStation (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) for quality assessment. All RNA samples were good quality with RNA Integrity Number (RIN) > 8.0 and were processed for mRNA-seq library preparation. RNase-free working environment was maintained, and RNase-free tips, tubes, and plates were utilized for the subsequent steps. Messenger RNA was selectively isolated from total RNA (300 ng input) using oligo(dT)25 magnetic beads according to the manufacturer’s guidelines in the NEBNext poly(A) mRNA magnetic isolation module (Cat. # E7490, NEB, Ipswich, MA). The library preparation from the enriched mRNA was conducted according to NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA kit (Cat. # E7760, NEB, Ipswich, MA). Brieﬂy, the enriched mRNA samples were chemically fragmented in a buffer containing divalent cations by heating to 94 °C for 15 min. The fragmented RNA was random hexamer primed and reverse transcribed to generate the ﬁrst strand of cDNA. The second strand was synthesized after removing the RNA template and incorporating dUTP in place of dTTP to maintain strand speciﬁcity. Fragmented ds cDNA was then end repaired and adenylated at their 3’ ends. A corresponding ‘T’ nucleotide on the adapters was utilized for ligating the adapter sequences to the cDNA. The adapter ligated DNA was puriﬁed using magnetic beads and PCR ampliﬁed (using 11 cycles) to incorporate a unique barcode and to generate the ﬁnal libraries. The ﬁnal libraries were puriﬁed using magnetic beads to remove any remaining primers and adapters. The ﬁnal libraries were validated on an Agilent 4200 TapeStation (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA), normalized to 4 nM, pooled equally, and loaded onto an Illumina NextSeq 2000 P3 100-cycle ﬂow cell (Cat. # 20040559, Illumina, San Diego, CA) at 750pM ﬁnal concentration and sequenced using 2 x 51 bp paired-end chemistry. On average we generated ~90 million reads pass ﬁlter (base quality score >Q30 suggesting less than 1 error in 1000 bp) per sample for 4 h and 14 day treatment groups.

We contracted Euroﬁns DiscoverX (Fremont, CA) to perform the scanMAX assay within the larger KINOMEscan™screening platform. KINOMEscan™assays do not require ATP and thereby report true thermodynamic interaction afﬁnities, as opposed to IC50 values, which can depend on the ATP concentration. The largest commercial kinase panel available, scanMAX contains a set of 468 kinases covering AGC, CAMK, CMGC, CK1, STE, TK, TKL, lipid and atypical kinase families, plus important mutant forms. scanMAX is an ideal choice for all stages of drug discovery and development, from lead discovery & hit identiﬁcation to lead optimization, preclinical and compound safety. Kinome-wide annotation of compound selectivity enables informed decisions about therapeutic opportunities and potential offtarget liabilities which could otherwise be missed in smaller kinase panels. This panel includes: 453 human kinases, 3 pathogen kinases, 56 disease relevant mutants, 132 tyrosine kinase assays, and 20 lipid kinases.

Kinase assays For most assays, kinase-tagged T7 phage strains were grown in parallel in 24-well blocks in an E. coli host derived from the BL21 strain. E. coli were grown to log-phase and infected with T7 phage from a frozen stock (multiplicity of infection = 0.4) and incubated with shaking at 32 °C until lysis (90-150 min). The lysates were centrifuged (6,000 x g) and ﬁltered (0.2 μm) to remove cell debris. The remaining kinases were produced in HEK-293 cells and subsequently tagged with DNA for qPCR detection. Streptavidin-coated magnetic beads were treated with biotinylated small molecule ligands for 30 min at room temperature to generate afﬁnity resins for kinase assays. The liganded beads were blocked with excess biotin and washed with blocking

buffer (SeaBlock (Pierce), 1 % BSA, 0.05 % Tween 20, 1 mM DTT) to remove unbound ligand and to reduce non-speciﬁc phage binding. Binding reactions were assembled by combining kinases, liganded afﬁnity beads, and test compounds in 1x binding buffer (20 % SeaBlock, 0.17x PBS, 0.05 % Tween 20, 6 mM DTT). Test compounds were prepared as 100x stocks in 100% DMSO and directly diluted into the assay. All reactions were performed in polypropylene 384-well plates in a ﬁnal volume of 0.02 mL. The assay plates were incubated at room temperature with shaking for 1 h and the afﬁnity beads were washed with wash buffer (1x PBS, 0.05 % Tween 20). The beads were then resuspended in elution buffer (1x PBS, 0.05 % Tween 20, 0.5 μM nonbiotinylated afﬁnity ligand) and incubated at room temperature with shaking for 30 min. The kinase concentration in the eluates was measured by qPCR.
